items.passage: Kaya had interpreted for Nneka for three years, and she would tell anyone who asked that the woman was impossible. Nneka changed her mind mid-sentence, made Kaya repeat whole contracts twice, and insisted, every Friday after their meetings, on stopping at the same shoe repair stall in Lagos to have the same left heel glued. The heel did not need gluing. Kaya said so, in two languages, to Nneka and to the cobbler. Neither listened. She would not have called the Fridays pleasant, not quite. Last week Nneka's company assigned a new interpreter, a young man with excellent references, and Nneka mentioned it in the car as though discussing the weather. Kaya said nothing. On Friday she went to the stall early, alone, paid the cobbler in advance for a month of heels, and left the receipt with Nneka's name on it.

Warm attachment to Nneka while acting from guilt over past complaints
Dry amusement at the heel repairs while dismissing them as wasted money
Quiet devotion to their shared habit while voicing steady complaint about it

items.passage:
Two rules for the crossing at the dry riverbed in Vermont:
step on the flat stones, and do not mention the trial.
Solange, retired from the bench, keeps the first rule loudly;
she lectures me on stones the way she once lectured juries,
and I roll my eyes behind her, as clerks are allowed to do.
Her rulings ran long. So do her walks.
I would not call this friendship, exactly.
The second rule we keep without a word.
Last week, halfway across, she slowed
where the old flood line still stains the bank,
the place where the case began.
I started talking about stones,
the gray ones, the split ones, the one shaped like a gavel,
and kept on talking until we reached the far side,
and offered my arm for the climb, which she took.
items.question: Which choice best describes the speaker's attitude toward Solange?
options: Protective loyalty toward her while keeping up a show of mild mockery
Mild impatience with her while enduring her lectures out of duty
Real respect for her while feeling guilty about the old trial
Fond interest in the stones while ignoring the flood line on the bank

items.passage: Brakes shrieked somewhere under the floor, and the compartment smelled of wet wool and the oranges my father had been peeling since we left Krakow. He had my article open on his knee again. For the third time that morning he was translating it, line by line, for Tatiana, a woman with a cello case who had made the mistake of asking where we were going. His Polish turned my four modest paragraphs into something closer to a speech. I told him the piece was about drainage policy and that no one on earth needed to hear it twice. He nodded and kept going. I was not embarrassed, exactly; I had simply heard the paragraph about storm grates often enough to recite it. At Tarnów, Tatiana got off, and my father folded the page into careful quarters. When he dozed against the window, I took the spare copy from my own bag, smoothed its creases, and tucked it into the pocket of his coat, beneath his ticket.

Touched by his attention while mostly regretting that she chose so dull a subject

items.passage: Oaxaca had been dry for weeks, and the gate of the community garden on Calle Murguía stayed padlocked past nine. Ximena waited with a sack of seedlings she had bought before she had anywhere to put them. A man in a straw hat, Emiliano, waited too. While they stood there he pointed out which beds belonged to whom, which faucet leaked, and which neighbor would lend a hoe if asked twice. He told her that the first month was the hardest and that the soil here forgave mistakes. On the fence beside them hung a tin sign with a plot number painted over in blue. Neither of them mentioned it. When the coordinator finally arrived, out of breath, she unlocked the gate and handed out two sets of keys. She asked Emiliano to sign the register under the heading for new members, just below the line where Ximena had written her name. He took off his hat to do it, then stood holding the pen a moment longer than the signature required.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: It presents a newcomer gathering practical advice from a helpful stranger during a delay.
It depicts two new members signing a garden register after a coordinator arrives late.
It shows how a stranger's advice prompts a newcomer to sign up as a garden member.
It reveals that a stranger's assured guidance came from someone hardly less unfamiliar there.

items.passage: Steam and blueing and the slap of wet cotton on stone: that was the laundry on Grant Road, and that was where Mohan taught me to fold. A sari, he said, had to be halved, then halved again, the border kept outward so a customer could see the work at once. He made me do it forty times one afternoon, until the creases lay flat as pressed leaves. 'One day these shelves are yours,' he said, and went back to his ledger. On the top shelf, behind the starch tins, sat a letter with a Poona postmark that nobody opened while I was in the room. Two years later I told him about the teaching post in Poona. He did not answer. That evening I found my trunk on the counter, already filled, every blouse and sari halved and halved again, borders turned outward, and the lid left open for me to close.

items.passage: Three rules governed Miss Kai's shop on Harbour Street: measure twice, cut once, and walk the sea wall every Sunday after chapel. The first two I understood. The third she never explained. Each week in that summer of 1861 we went along the promenade at Kingston, she with her parasol, I a step behind with my hands still smelling of chalk, and each week she stopped at the same iron bench to watch the fishing boats come in. 'When you keep a shop of your own,' she said once, 'you will know why.' In her workroom lay a bolt of blue linen that she dusted but did not cut. Thirty years on, my own shop has a sign over the door and a boy who threads needles faster than I ever did. On Sundays he walks a step behind me. I stop at the iron bench. He has not yet asked why, and I have not yet decided what I would tell him.

It shows how a mentor's unexplained Sunday habit has passed into the narrator's own life.

It suggests that the narrator's apprentice led him to recall his mentor's weekly walk.

items.passage: Receipts curled from the printer every few minutes at the all-night pharmacy on Długa Street, and Valentina tore each one off without looking. A year earlier, on the night her brother Suhyun left for his posting, he had borrowed her grey scarf for the bus to the barracks. She had texted him about it twice in the first month, once with a photograph of the empty hook by her door, and then had stopped. Her mother still asked whether he had answered. At ten past three one February morning, the door chimed. Suhyun stood by the cough syrups in a coat too thin for the Baltic wind, the grey scarf wound twice around his throat. Its fringe had been knotted back where it frayed, and one end was darned in thread a shade too dark. He set a packet of lozenges on the counter and reached for his wallet. Valentina pushed the coins back across to him.

It depicts a late-night meeting between a pharmacist and her brother back from service.

It suggests that a sister's messages about a scarf led her brother to keep away.

items.passage: Somchai never turned off the kitchen light. Every night at eleven she filled a glass of water, set it on the oilcloth beside the bread tin, and left the bulb burning over the stove. When the landlady complained about the bill, Somchai said the fuse box in that corner tripped whenever the switch was touched, and that she would rather pay than climb a ladder in the dark. The landlady let it go. The light had first stayed on in March, two nights after Karim was brought home by a taxi driver who had found him at the Charles Helou bus station holding a folded map of the southern roads. That same week the map disappeared from its nail in the hall. At two in the morning, Karim's slippers shuffled down the corridor, paused at the bright doorway, and turned in. Somchai, awake in the next room, listened to a chair scrape and a glass set down.

To draw Karim toward a settled room before he could head out to the street
To keep up a nightly routine of preparing the kitchen before she went to bed
To make amends for having let Karim leave the house unnoticed in March

items.passage: Folding chairs clattered onto the deck as my mother counted them aloud, one for each table she had already drawn on the back of a calendar. Every year on my birthday, since I was six, Yuxuan had taken me out on this same barge on the Tamsui, bought two bowls of fish-ball soup, and let me lean over the rail. Now she wanted my wedding banquet here. 'The good restaurant halls are booked until spring,' she said, when I asked. 'This is simpler, Jiayi.' I believed her until I opened the tea tin in her kitchen to find the sugar. Under the lid lay a deposit slip from the barge company, stamped in ink gone brown, dated 1977, my name on the back. I was seven that year and had not yet met anyone I would marry. I put the lid back. On the day itself, my mother walked to the stern before the guests arrived and tied a strip of red cloth around the third rail post.
items.question: Based on the text, why does Yuxuan most likely insist on holding the banquet on the barge?

To continue the birthday outings she had shared with her daughter for years
To honor an arrangement she had made for her daughter during childhood
To avoid the cost of a formal hall that she feared she could not pay

items.passage: Rain drums on the galvanized roof, and the lamp smells of coconut oil and scorched wick. Each night Roshane sits across from you and copies your pages into his ledger, the French on the left, your English on the right, his pen scratching long after you have gone to bed. You had expected him to arrive with objections; his own novels sold better than yours in Paris. When you ask why he has not gone back down to Port of Spain, Linton, he says the road below the cocoa estate is washed out. Perhaps it is. Yet the boy who brought his mule up the hill led it home on Tuesday, a full day before the first rain. And the publisher's letter, the one asking for forty pages to be cut, is no longer on the shelf where you left it. On Sunday morning you find his finished ledger beside your inkwell, every chapter intact, its spine tied with your own blue ribbon.
items.question: Based on the text, why does Roshane most likely remain at the cottage?
options: To wait until the washed-out road below the estate could be crossed again
To keep up his nightly practice of copying the pages as fast as he could
To make up for the sales in which his novels had outpaced the author's
To complete a full version of the book before any requested cuts were made

items.passage: We arrived at the Posillipo pool at seven, because Elisa said the salt water was flattest before the swim club came. My brother brought goggles. She confiscated them. Her method had four parts, which she listed like train stops: lie back, ears under, hands open, stop trying. Fishermen's sons had learned it on this coast before anyone sold inflatable rings, she said, and now the sons sold inflatable rings. My brother sank eleven times.
